201: Hill continues explaining the elevated state of thought. While on this exalted plane, the individual is like one who has ascended in an airplane—seeing objects beyond the horizon that limits ground-level vision. The person is not hampered by stimuli that circumscribe vision while wrestling with food, clothing, and shelter necessities. The creative faculty is given freedom for action; the Sixth Sense becomes receptive to ideas unreachable under other circumstances. The Sixth Sense is the defining faculty marking the difference between a genius and an ordinary individual. The more this faculty is used, the more alert and receptive it becomes to thought vibrations originating outside the subconscious mind. This faculty can be cultivated only through use. Conscience operates entirely through the Sixth Sense. Great artists, writers, musicians, and poets become great because they acquire the habit of relying upon the 'still small voice' speaking from within through Creative Imagination. Hill shares examples: a great orator who closes his eyes before climaxes, saying 'I speak through ideas which come to me from within,' and a famous financier who closed his eyes for two or three minutes before decisions, saying 'With my eyes closed, I am able to draw upon a source of superior intelligence.'
202: Hill presents Dr. Elmer R. Gates of Chevy Chase, Maryland, who created more than 200 useful patents through cultivating and using the creative faculty. Gates had a 'personal communication room'—practically soundproof with all light shut out, equipped with a table and writing pad. When desiring to draw upon Creative Imagination, he would enter the room, sit at the table, lower the lights, and CONCENTRATE upon the KNOWN factors of his invention, remaining until ideas began flashing into his mind regarding the UNKNOWN factors. On one occasion, ideas came so fast he wrote continuously for almost three hours. When thoughts stopped, his notes contained descriptions of principles with no parallel among known scientific data, with the answer intelligently presented. In this manner, Gates completed over 200 patents begun but not completed by less resourceful inventors. He earned his living by 'sitting for ideas' for corporations, which paid substantial hourly fees. Hill notes the normal faculty of reason is often faulty because guided by accumulated experience, which isn't always accurate. Ideas received through the creative faculty are more reliable because they come from more reliable sources. The major difference between a genius and an ordinary 'crank' inventor is that the genius works through Creative Imagination while the crank knows nothing of this faculty.
203: Hill explains that the scientific inventor (like Edison or Gates) uses both synthetic and creative faculties. The genius-mode inventor begins by organizing and combining known ideas through the synthetic faculty (reasoning). If accumulated knowledge is insufficient, the inventor draws upon the creative faculty. The procedure: (1) THEY STIMULATE THEIR MINDS so the brain functions on a higher-than-average plane and intensity, using one or more of the ten mind stimulants. (2) THEY CONCENTRATE upon the known factors (finished part) of their invention and create a perfect mental picture of unknown factors (unfinished part), holding this picture until the subconscious takes it over, then relaxing and clearing the mind of ALL thought, waiting for the answer to flash. Results may be definite and immediate or negative, depending on Sixth Sense development. Edison tried more than 10,000 combinations through the synthetic faculty before tuning in through the creative faculty to get the answer that perfected the incandescent light. His experience was similar with the phonograph. Hill notes reliable evidence of Creative Imagination exists through analysis of leaders who achieved greatness without extensive educations. Lincoln is a notable example—he discovered and began using this faculty as a result of the stimulation of love after meeting Anne Rutledge, a statement of the highest significance regarding the source of genius.
204: Hill states the pages of history are filled with records of great leaders whose achievements trace directly to the influence of their beloved, who aroused their creative faculties through stimulation of sex desire. Napoleon Bonaparte was irresistible and invincible when inspired by his first wife Josephine. When his 'better judgment' prompted him to put Josephine aside, he began to decline—his defeat and St. Helena were not far distant. Hill notes he could mention scores of well-known Americans who climbed to great heights under their spouses' stimulating influence, only to drop back to destruction after casting aside their original loves. Napoleon was not the only person to discover that sex influence from the right source is more powerful than any substitute of expediency created by mere reason. The human mind responds to stimulation, and among the most powerful stimuli is the sexual urge. When harnessed and transmuted, this driving force lifts individuals into a higher sphere of thought, enabling them to master worry and petty annoyance. Unfortunately, only geniuses have made this discovery. Hill then lists outstanding achievers known to have had highly developed sexual natures, beginning with George Washington and Napoleon Bonaparte.
205: Hill continues the list of outstanding achievers known for highly developed sexual natures: William Shakespeare, Abraham Lincoln, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Robert Burns, Thomas Jefferson, Elbert Hubbard, Elbert H. Gary, Oscar Wilde, Woodrow Wilson, John H. Patterson, Andrew Jackson, and Enrico Caruso. He challenges readers to find a single individual in all history who achieved outstanding success in any calling who was not driven by a well-developed sexual nature. If not relying on biographies of the deceased, take inventory of living great achievers and see if any lacks high sexual energy. Sexual energy is the creative energy of virtually all geniuses—there never has been and never will be a great leader, builder, or artist lacking this driving force. However, not all who are highly sexed are geniuses. Individuals attain genius status ONLY when they stimulate their mind to draw upon forces available through the creative faculty. The mere possession of sex energy is insufficient—it must be transmuted from desire for physical contact into other forms of desire and action. Far from becoming geniuses, the majority lower themselves through misunderstanding and misuse of this great force to the status of lower animals.
206: Under 'Why Most People Seldom Succeed Before 40,' Hill shares his analysis of more than 25,000 people: individuals who succeed outstandingly seldom do so before age 40, and more often don't strike their real pace until well beyond 50. This prompted 12 years of careful study. The major reason: most people DISSIPATE their energies through overindulgence in the physical expression of sex. Most never learn that the sexual urge has other possibilities far transcending mere physical expression. Those who do make this discovery do so after wasting many years during peak sexual energy (prior to 45-50), usually followed by noteworthy achievement. The lives of many up to and past 40 reflect continued dissipation of energies that could have been channeled better—their finer emotions are 'sown wildly to the four winds,' giving rise to the term 'sowing one's wild oats.' The desire for sexual expression is the strongest and most impelling of all human emotions, and when harnessed and transmuted, may lift one into the 'genius mode.' History shows some attained genius status with artificial stimulants: Edgar Allan Poe wrote 'The Raven' under the influence of liquor, James Whitcomb Riley did amazing writing under alcohol, and Robert Burns wrote 'For Auld Lang Syne' under intoxicants.
207: Hill cautions that many who used artificial stimulants destroyed themselves in the end. Nature has prepared her own potions—deep love, sexual drive, and the power of autosuggestion—with which people may safely stimulate their minds to function on a higher plane. No satisfactory substitute for Nature's natural stimulants has ever been found. The world is ruled and civilization's destiny established by human emotions—people are influenced by feelings, not reason. The creative faculty is set into action entirely by emotions, not cold reason. The most powerful of all human emotions is sex. A mind stimulant is any influence that increases the freedom, intensity, and concentration of thought. Through the 10 Mind Stimuli, one may commune with Infinite Intelligence or enter the subconscious mind storehouse at will—this is all there is of genius. Hill shares a teacher's discovery that individuals with high sex drives generally make the most efficient salespeople. Personal magnetism is nothing more nor less than sex energy. This vital force may be communicated to others through: (1) the handshake—touch indicates instantly the presence or absence of magnetism; (2) the tone of voice—magnetism colors the voice, making it musical and charming; (3) posture and carriage—highly sexual people move briskly with grace and ease.
208: Hill continues how sex energy is communicated to others: (4) the vibrations of thought—highly sexual people mix the emotion of sex with their thoughts, influencing those around them; (5) body adornment—people with high sex drives are usually very careful about personal appearance, selecting clothing becoming to their personality. When employing salespeople, capable sales managers look for personal magnetism as the first requirement. People lacking sex energy will never become enthusiastic nor inspire others, and enthusiasm is one of the most important requisites in salesmanship. The public speaker, orator, preacher, lawyer, or salesperson lacking sex energy is generally a flop at influencing others. Most people can be influenced only through an appeal to their emotions. Top salespeople attain mastery because they consciously or unconsciously transmute sex energy into SALES ENTHUSIASM. Salespeople who take their mind off sex itself and direct that energy into sales effort—with enthusiasm and determination—have already acquired the art of sex transmutation whether they know it or not. Transmutation calls for more willpower than the average person cares to use, but the reward is worth the effort. The entire subject of sex is one about which the majority are unpardonably ignorant—the sexual urge has been grossly misunderstood, slandered, and burlesqued for so long that the very word 'sex' has taken on lascivious and sordid connotations.
209: Hill notes that men and women blessed with high sex drives are frequently looked upon with suspicion and contempt, considered abnormal and base rather than normal, healthy, and blessed. Millions have inferiority complexes developed from the false belief that a high sex drive is a curse. Yet statements about sexual energy's virtue should not be construed as justification for the libertine. The emotion of sex is a virtue ONLY when used intelligently and with discrimination—it may be misused to debase both body and mind. Hill discovered that practically every great leader he analyzed was a person whose achievements were largely inspired by someone they loved deeply—often a modest, self-denying spouse of whom the public had heard little. Intemperance in sex habits is as detrimental as intemperance in drinking and eating. Sexual intemperance is common in our age, which may help account for the relative shortage of great leaders. No individual can avail themselves of Creative Imagination while dissipating its forces. Human beings are the only creatures that violate Nature's purpose in this connection—every other animal indulges its sexual nature in moderation and 'in season.' Humans declare 'open season.' Every intelligent person knows that stimulation in excess through alcohol and narcotics destroys vital organs including the brain. Not everyone knows that overindulgence in sexual expression may become a habit as destructive to creative effort as narcotics or liquor. A sex-obsessed individual is not essentially different from a drug addict—both have lost control over reason and willpower.
210: Hill warns that sexual overindulgence may lead to temporary or permanent mental dysfunction, and many cases of hypochondria (imaginary illness) grow out of habits developed in ignorance of sex's true function. Ignorance of sex transmutation forces stupendous penalties upon the ignorant while withholding tremendous benefits. Widespread ignorance is due to the subject being surrounded with mystery and dark silence—the conspiracy of mystery has had the same effect on young people's minds that prohibition psychology had, increasing curiosity and desire for forbidden knowledge. To the shame of lawmakers and physicians—who are best qualified to educate youth—appropriate information has all too often not been made available. Hill states that seldom does an individual enter upon highly creative effort before 40. The average person reaches greatest capacity to create between 40 and 60. These statements, based on observation and analysis of thousands, should encourage those who fail to arrive before 40 and those frightened at approaching old age. The years between 40 and 50 are the most fruitful. Henry Ford had not hit his pace until past 40. Andrew Carnegie was well past 40 before reaping rewards. James J. Hill was still running a telegraph key at 40—his stupendous achievements came after. Between 30 and 40, people begin to learn the art of sex transmutation, generally accidentally and unconsciously.
